questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Equation of a Tangent Plane
questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=y\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1$ at the point $(1,1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1) \\  & =\frac{y}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1) & =\frac{1}{1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{1}{1}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-1 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1) \\ z-1 & =1\cdot (x-1)+1\cdot (y-1) \\ z-1 & =x+y-2 \\ -x-y+z+1 & =0 \\ x+y-z-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=\operatorname{arctan}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{y}^{3}$ at the point $(2,0,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{y}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{({x}^{2}y)^{2}+1}\cdot 2xy \\  & =\frac{2xy}{{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{y}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{({x}^{2}y)^{2}+1}\cdot {x}^{2}-3{y}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1}-3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(2,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,0) & =\frac{2(2)(0)}{(2)^{4}(0)^{2}+1}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,0) & =\frac{(2)^{2}}{(2)^{4}(0)^{2}+1}-3(0)^{2}=4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-0 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,0)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,0) \\ z & =0(x-0)+4(y-0) \\ z & =4y \\ 4y-z & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Determine the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}+3$ at the point $(0,1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}+3) \\  & =2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}+3) \\  & =-4y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(0,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,1) & =2(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,1) & =-4(1)=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-1 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,1) \\ z-1 & =0x-4(y-1) \\ z-1 & =-4y+4 \\ 4y+z-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={y}^{2}{e}^{2x}-1$ at the point $(0,2,3).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}{e}^{2x}-1) \\  & =2{y}^{2}{e}^{2x} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}{e}^{2x}-1) \\  & =2y{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(0,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,2) & =2(2)^{2}{e}^{2(0)}=8 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,2) & =2(2){e}^{2(0)}=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-3 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,2) \\ z-3 & =8(x-0)+4(y-2) \\ z-3 & =8x+4y-8 \\ -8x-4y+z+5 & =0 \\ 8x+4y-z-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=\sqrt{xy}+xy$ at the point $(2,2,6).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xy}+xy) \\  & =\frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy}}+y \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{y}}{2\sqrt{x}}+y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xy}+xy) \\  & =\frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy}}+x \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{y}}+x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(2,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+2=\frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+2=\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-6 & =(x-2)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2) \\ z-6 & =\frac{5}{2}(x-2)+\frac{5}{2}(y-2) \\ z-6 & =\frac{5x}{2}+\frac{5y}{2}-10 \\ 2z-12 & =5x+5y-20 \\ -5x-5y+2z+8 & =0 \\ 5x+5y-2z-8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz)$ at the point $(-1,1,1,-\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xz}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xy}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1) & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1\cdot 1)=\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-(-\pi ) & =(x-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi (x+1)-2(y-1)-2(z-1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi x-2y-2z+4+\pi  \\ \pi x-2y-2z-w+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Equation of a Tangent Hyperplane
questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)$ at the point $(1,1,\pi ,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,\pi ):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,\pi )+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,\pi )+(z-\pi )\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,\pi ) \\ w & =-\pi (x-1)-\pi (y-1)-(z-\pi ) \\ w & =-\pi x+\pi -\pi y+\pi -z+\pi  \\ \pi x+\pi y+z+w-3\pi  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx}$ at the point $(2,2,2,6).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{y}}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{\sqrt{z}}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{y}}+\frac{\sqrt{z}}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{y}}{2\sqrt{z}}+\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(2,2,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-6 & =(x-2)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,2)+(z-2)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,2) \\ w-6 & =(x-2)+(y-2)+(z-2) \\ w-6 & =x+y+z-6 \\ -x-y-z+w & =0 \\ x+y+z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=z\sqrt{y}-x$ at the point $(-1,4,1,3).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z\sqrt{y}-x)=-1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(z\sqrt{y}-x)=\frac{z}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(z\sqrt{y}-x)=\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(-1,4,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,4,1) & =-1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,4,1) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,4,1) & =\sqrt{4}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-3 & =(x-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,4,1)+(y-4)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,4,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,4,1) \\ w-3 & =-(x+1)+\frac{1}{4}(y-4)+2(z-1) \\ w-3 & =-x+\frac{1}{4}y+2z-4 \\ x-\frac{1}{4}y-2z+w+1 & =0 \\ 4x-y-8z+4w+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z}$ at the point $(1,9,4,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,9,4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{9}}=\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}=-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-2 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4)+(y-9)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4)+(z-4)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1)+\frac{1}{6}(y-9)-\frac{1}{4}(z-4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1 & =0 \\ 12(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1) & =12\cdot 0 \\ 6x+2y-3z-12w+12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z={x}^{3}+xy$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+xy)=3{x}^{2}+y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+xy)=x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨3{x}^{2}+y,\,x,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+y=0 \\ x=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the second equation we get $x=0.$ Substituting $x=0$ into first equation, we obtain $y=0.$

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z={0}^{3}+0(0)=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy) \\  & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y,\,-x,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y,\,-x,\,-1⟩=⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2c\operatorname{cos}⁡x-cy=8 \\ -xc=2\pi  \\ -c=2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
-x(-2)=2\pi \,⟹\,x=\pi .
$$

And substituting $c=-2$ and $x=\pi $ into the first equation, we have 

$$
2(-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -(-2)y=8\,⟹\,y=2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\pi $ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -(\pi )(2) \\  & =-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector  $v$ at $(\pi ,2,-2\pi ).$

questions.problem:
At which points on the surface $z=4{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-6$  is the tangent plane 
horizontal?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-6) \\  & =8xy+{y}^{3} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{3}-6) \\  & =4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨8xy+{y}^{3},\,4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}8xy+{y}^{3}=0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+3x{y}^{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $y=0$ or ${y}^{2}+8x=0.$ So, we have two cases.

- If $y=0$, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
4{x}^{2}+3x(0)^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=0.
$$

- If ${y}^{2}=-8x$, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
4{x}^{2}+3x(-8x)^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=0.
$$

Substituting $x=0$ back into ${y}^{2}=-8x$ gives

$$
{y}^{2}=-8(0)\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

So, in both cases, we have $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Finally, substituting these values into our function, we get

$$
z=4(0)^{2}(0)+(0)(0)^{3}-6=-6.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,-6).$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨-2,4,2⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & ={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =x{e}^{y}+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,4,2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,4,2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}c{e}^{y}=-2 \\ cx{e}^{y}+2cy=4 \\ -c=2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-2{e}^{y}=-2\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

And substituting $c=-2$ and $y=0$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-2x{e}^{0}+2(-2)(0)=4\,⟹\,x=-2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-2$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2} \\  & =(-2){e}^{0}+{0}^{2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-2,0,-2).$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z={x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2x-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2y+6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x-2,\,2y+6,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}2x-2=0 \\ 2y+6=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=1$ while the second equation gives $y=-3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=1$ and $y=-3$ into our function, we get

$$
z={1}^{2}-2(1)+(-3)^{2}+6(-3)+10=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(1,-3,0).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z= x^2 + xy$ at the point $(1,2, 3).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2x+y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy) \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (1,2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2) & =2(1)+2=4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-3 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) \\ z-3 & =4(x-1)+1(y-2) \\ z-3 & =4x+y-6 \\ -4x-y+z+3 & =0 \\ 4x+y-z-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=x^2+y^2+z^2-2xyz$ at the point $(1,-1,1,5).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0,w_0)$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w - w_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (z-z_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x_0,y_0,z_0).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2x-2yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2y-2xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2z-2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z) = (1,-1,1)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1) & =2(1)-2(-1)(1)=4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1) & =2(-1)-2(1)(1)=-4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) & =2(1)-2(1)(-1)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-5 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1)+(y+1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}w-5 & =4(x-1)-4(y+1)+4(z-1) \\ w-5 & =4x-4y+4z-12 \\ -4x+4y-4z+w+7 & =0 \\ 4x-4y+4z-w-7 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: At which points on the surface $z={y^2}+ {xy}$  is the tangent plane horizontal?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The tangent plane to a surface is horizontal if and only if the normal vector to the tangent plane is vertical. So, let's first find the general expression of a normal vector to the surface.

Remember that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)
$$

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2y+x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, a normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
\left\langle y, \: 2y+x, \: -1 \right\rangle.
$$

We want to find where this normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064554/assets/a20e553b10de1d00abd5beead7766a1859073f07b1f5bfb734b51e8433fbeee0.png) 

From the first equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
2(0) +x = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = 0.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z = 0^2+(0)(0)= 0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$
